articles.title: A rural Idaho county banned renewables. It’s having second thoughts.
articles.author: Julia Tilton, The Daily Yonder
paras: Jeff Hough did not pull any punches. What his fellow Republican county commissioners were about to do, he said to the packed courthouse, would violate America’s founding ideals. He quoted the Declaration of Independence to make his case.
The three-person commission was about to vote on an ordinance that would ban utility-scale solar and wind development in Bannock County, Idaho.
“We cannot deny the entire county the opportunity to exercise their property rights,” Hough said. “That goes against the principles this country was founded on.”
A few minutes after Hough’s emphatic speech , the ordinance passed by a 2–1 vote. Hough was the lone dissenter.

Since that consequential vote in March 2024, Hough has become the chair of the county commission and has dedicated himself to overturning that ordinance. He will soon have a chance to make that happen. This fall, Hough and the other two commissioners are set to vote on an ordinance with new language that would allow the development of solar and wind, along with nuclear energy, in the county.
The Bannock County vote is a test case of whether — and how — a community can revisit its assumptions about the costs and benefits of clean energy and decide to welcome development it once swore off.

In 2025, nearly 1 in 4 U.S. counties had some kind of ban, moratorium, or impediment to clean energy development, up from 15 percent of counties in 2023. More than 60 percent of counties with bans are rural, according to a Daily Yonder and Canary Media analysis of data from USA Today and the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University. (The Daily Yonder defines “rural” using criteria from the U.S. Office of Management and Budget .)

Bucking this national trend and reversing the ban would put Bannock County back in play at a moment when Idaho needs all the energy it can get. Idaho Power , the state’s largest utility, expects electricity demand to grow by 1 gigawatt by 2030, a roughly 26 percent leap from current levels.

“The need to build stuff now is critical to Idaho’s economic future,” said Aaron Menenberg, the Idaho policy manager for Renewable Northwest, a nonprofit working to decarbonize the region’s grid. “We can’t afford to say no to anything.”

Bannock County, nestled in a valley a few hours north of Salt Lake City and 100 miles west of Wyoming’s Teton Range, is a prime location for new power plants. It’s home to the Populus substation, a critical juncture for getting electrons onto the grid and into Idaho, Utah, Wyoming, and the Pacific Northwest. Building new power plants near a substation is cheaper, and those savings can help bring down costs for utility customers.

But the biggest opportunity for county residents, as Hough sees it, is not utility-bill savings: It’s economic development. In recent years, Bannock County’s population has grown far more slowly than Idaho’s. The county’s rural communities, meanwhile, are watching essential services disappear, and drought worsened by climate change is making it difficult for family farms to stay afloat.

Hough believes renewables would bring money into the community. Bannock County’s neighbors offer local proof: In 2024, projects in nearby Power and Bingham counties generated $909,000 and $639,000 in tax revenue, respectively. Hough wants to send a message — to the renewables industry and others — that Bannock County is “open for business,” too.

“Rural America is in a transition state,” Hough said from his office in Pocatello, the county seat, in July. “How do we make or help rural America … transition to this new way of life, so that they can thrive and prosper?”

Not everyone shares Hough’s vision of prosperity. In south Bannock County, Hough’s campaign has met with fierce opposition. Two camps exist: On one side are residents who are willing to lease their own land to solar energy developers or stand by their neighbors’ right to do so. On the other are those who are skeptical of renewables and believe that leasing land to developers is equivalent to selling out — many of them do, however, support nuclear.

Steve Criddle, a third-generation farmer and lifelong resident of south Bannock County, voiced his support for solar in 2024 before the ban passed. He described the situation today simply: “It’s confrontational.”
Bannock County’s moratorium on solar and wind stemmed from an unlikely source: Hough himself .
It was the fall of 2023, and he had just attended a conference of the Idaho Association of Counties in Boise.

At the conference, the Lava Ridge Wind Project , a 1-GW development slated for more than 57,000 acres of federal land in southern Idaho, dominated the conversation. County leaders from around the state were concerned about clean energy developers running roughshod over their communities. (President Donald Trump’s Interior Department canceled Lava Ridge in August 2025.)

The discussion got Hough thinking. Months before the conference, he had learned that several developers, including Chicago-based Hecate Energy and Moab, Utah–based Balanced Rock Power , were approaching landowners about solar projects in Bannock County.
When Hough returned from Boise, the cautionary tale of Lava Ridge fresh in his mind, he took action.
“I realized that we didn’t have any kind of ordinance,” Hough said. “So I knew they’d come in and do whatever they wanted.”

On October 12, 2023, spearheaded by Hough, the county commissioners voted unanimously to enact a six-month moratorium on large-scale energy projects. The idea was not to ban solar and wind, but simply to give the county time to regulate the developments and ensure they balanced economic opportunity with responsible land stewardship. A public hearing on the topic was set for the following February, and the commissioners would vote on the future of the moratorium in March.
But Hough’s moratorium took on a life of its own. In the months that followed, a group of concerned residents organized to make it permanent.

Rebecca Falcon led the charge. A decades-long resident of Downey, a town in south Bannock County, Falcon had been approached by Balanced Rock in September 2023 about leasing a portion of her 80 acres for solar. Appalled, she turned the company away. But Balanced Rock’s proposed Harmon Solar Project (aka Harmon I), a 300-megawatt solar facility with a 1,200-megawatt-hour on-site battery energy storage system, included her neighbors’ land. Stopping it would take more than just Falcon saying no.

Falcon and another neighbor, Dez Hauser, who had also turned away Balanced Rock, encouraged other concerned community members to show up to the February 2024 public hearing about the future of the moratorium.

By the time the hearing rolled around, residents had sorted themselves into two groups: for solar and against it. The meeting attracted such interest that it was moved from the county courthouse to a local high school auditorium in south Bannock County. The venue was still packed.
More than two dozen speakers, nearly all of them from south Bannock County, showed up to say their piece. The vast majority testified in opposition to solar.

The commissioners convened the next month to decide what to do with the moratorium. Hough voted to repeal it. The other two commissioners voted to extend it. The commissioners framed it as an additional pause to study the potential effects of large-scale renewable energy development in the county. Yet as the controversy mounted through the spring and summer of 2024, the county declined to take further action.
The ban stayed in place. Falcon, Hauser, and the other opponents had won.

Dale Lish, a grain farmer based in Downey, was frustrated with the decision. Recently retired from a career at the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Lish became familiar with solar while working on projects in Idaho and Washington through the Rural Energy for America Program. He spoke in favor of the energy source at the same hearing where Falcon and Hauser expressed their concerns.

“The approach was just no to everything, which bothered me,” Lish said of the county’s decision, in a June interview on his property. “A straight-out ban — I don’t think that’s American. I think we, as private-property owners, ought to have a chance to do what we want within reason.”
In 2023, Lish signed a one-year contract with Hecate to option about 400 acres of his land for solar development. Hecate declined to renew the contract in 2024 because of the county’s ordinance.
The company has since pulled out of the county altogether. Representatives from Hecate did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

For the two and a half years since that March vote, Hough has been beating the drum of private-property rights while also trying to educate the community on Idaho’s power needs and how they might be met in Bannock County.

While the commission won’t vote until later this fall on the new ordinance, which is still undergoing public review, at least one of Hough’s colleagues may have changed his tune. Ernie Moser, an incumbent who supported the ban in 2024, said in an interview in June that his fears about solar and wind are “not as big” as they were two years ago. Still, Moser, who’s retiring from the commission at the end of this year, stressed that he wants “to do it right” when it comes to revisiting the county’s energy policy. The other commissioner, Ken Bullock, declined to comment.

May’s primary elections offered another indication of the county’s divided views. In the Republican primary, Hough faced a challenger from south Bannock County with an anti-solar platform, and though he won his race by 14 percentage points overall, his opponent captured 70 percent of the vote in Downey. No Democrat is running in the race, so Hough won’t face competition in the November general election.
This year’s results mirror those of 2024, when former county commissioner John Crowder, who voted for the ban in March of that year, won big in Downey but lost to Ken Bullock, an ally of Hough’s.
“In south Bannock County, it’s a supermajority of residents that do not want this,” Crowder said about solar development.

Steve Criddle can trace his family’s roots in Downey back to 1876, when his ancestors first filed paperwork for water rights. His grandfather farmed grain, including wheat. Criddle’s father did the same. He’s kept the agricultural heritage alive himself, but because of a changing climate, grain farming is no longer enough to sustain him.

“We don’t get enough moisture anymore,” Criddle said. The fields where he grows crops without irrigation now hardly produce enough to make ends meet. He’s turned some of his land over to cattle grazing and has worked odd jobs over the years to hold on to the farm.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: New Train Day!
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: 2026 has been a big year for trains in Puget Sound. In January, the Federal Way Link Extension completed its first full month of operation. Simulated service on the 2 Line began in February , providing 4 minute frequencies for the first time between Seattle and Lynnwood. In March, the Crosslake Connection finally connected the 2 Line with Seattle. Link ridership jumped 46% in April thanks to the new service across Lake Washington. In May, the Sound Transit Board confirmed funding for several ST3 Link extensions (at the cost of other extensions). In June, Sound Transit welcomed passengers aboard new Sounder trains and set multiple Link ridership records . The USA vs Belgium World Cup match in early July helped Link surpass 300,000 passengers in one day for the first time ever. Last month, transit agencies in Snohomish, King, and Pierce counties restructured their bus networks to cement Link as the backbone for regional transportation in Puget Sound.
To add to the list, Sound Transit is opening a new Link station and Amtrak is rolling out next-generation trains in September.

On September 30, Amtrak Cascades will welcome the first passengers aboard new Amtrak Airo trainsets. Amtrak Airo are trains built by Siemens that will soon run on many short distance Amtrak routes across the country. The first three of eight trains for the Cascades route are in Seattle and will operate on two roundtrips daily. The remaining five trainsets will enter service as they complete testing. An additional 75 Amtrak Airo trainsets will begin serving other routes around the country next year.

While the new trains will not reduce travel times or offer more daily trips, these trains can carry more passengers (over 300 seats per train), will be more reliable, and are more comfortable than the aging rolling stock currently used on Amtrak Cascades. Passengers can expect adjustable headrests, panoramic windows, enhanced lighting, and modern interiors.
Beginning September 30, Amtrak Airo trains will be used on the following Amtrak Cascades trips.
Between Seattle and Eugene: Train 503: Seattle to Eugene at 7:10am – 1:48pm Train 508: Eugene to Seattle at 4:30pm – 10:50pm
Between Seattle and Vancouver: Train 516: Seattle to Vancouver, B.C. at 8:30am – 12:30pm Train 519: Vancouver, B.C. to Seattle at 4:45pm – 9:10pm

Seattle Transit Blog will share a first look at the Amtrak Airo trains on Tuesday, including pictures and videos from a trip on the train. Until then, check out this Bluesky thread with highlights from the media tour on Saturday.

Also on September 30, Sound Transit will begin service at Pinehurst station. Pinehurst station is the agency’s first Link in-fill station and is located between Northgate and Shoreline South/148th stations. This the second piece of the ST3 measure to be completed (after Downtown Redmond Link) and will be the last Link station to open until Graham Street station in 2031. Pinehurst station is served by the new Metro Route 77 which connects the station with Bitter Lake and Lake City. 1 Line and 2 Line trains will begin stopping at Pinehurst station at 5am on September 30. The very first train to serve Pinehurst is a 2 Line train that departs Wilburton at 4:04am and arrives at Pinehurst at 5:05am.

To celebrate the new station, Sound Transit is hosting an event from 2pm-6pm on Wednesday. The event will include live music, local organizations, sponsors, food, an interactive activity with station artist Romson Bustillo, and the ST Shop merchandise booth.

articles.title: The flock thickens: Starbird Chicken is coming to Capitol Hill
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: $5 A MONTH TO HELP KEEP CHS PAYWALL-FREE Subscribe to CHS to help hire writers and photographers to cover the neighborhood. CHS is a pay what you can community news site with no required sign-in or paywall. To stay that way, we need you. Become a subscriber to help us cover the neighborhood for $5 a month -- or choose your level of support (Image: Starbird Chicken)

The mystery of new commercial life hatching in the failed 10,000-square-foot Amazon grocery on E Pike has been revealed. The arrival of Starbird Chicken on Capitol Hill will mark new energy for a block that has been darkened for two and a half years.

It will also be an example of what happens when highly optimized, fully leveraged, and fluidly designed corporate strategies cross lines, overlap, and push all their eggs into the same basket in a neighborhood with finger lickin good demographics and spending habits.

“Starbird has built something truly special by reimagining what a chicken restaurant can be, from the bold flavors and hospitable, modern restaurant design to the overall guest experience,” Vin Mehta , the Portland-based entrepreneur and franchisee leading a 17 location expansion of the chicken chain into the Pacific Northwest, said in a company press release quoted by industry tracker FastCasual.com . “Together, we’ll combine Starbird’s innovative approach with our team’s operational experience and passion for building lasting connections.”

CHS reported this summer on signs of new life in the Pike at Belmont space in the AVA Capitol Hill mixed-use redevelopment of the neighborhood’s old Mercedes-Benz dealership where the massive Amazon Go was abruptly shuttered in 2024 as part of what would become a nationwide retreat for the global giant.

This week, Starbird’s construction team filed new paperwork with details of their plans for a new 3,000-square-foot restaurant to serve the company’s tenders, wings, and sandwiches in a major chunk of the former cashier-less, tech-powered grocery space. An ambitious $620,000 base construction budget is attached.
The expansion has already been on the burner. A West Seattle Starbird is scheduled for its ribbon cutting on Fauntleroy Way SW on Monday .

Starbird is a Northern California-born, premium fast-casual restaurant chain founded in 2016 by culinary incubator The Culinary Edge , a company that operates as a gun for hire in revamping menus and operations for large national chains while also establishing its own brands.

Starbird specializes in “fresh, scratch-made food” and “always antibiotic-free, never frozen” fried chicken including tenders, sandwiches, wings, and “house-made sauces,” positioning itself around “reinventing the fast-food experience” with “feel good crispy chicken.” With an emphasis on “tech-enabled, omnichannel dining” and virtual kitchens alongside brick-and-mortar restaurants, the brand has expanded beyond California through multi-unit franchise partnerships.
The name also has a familiar ring. Yes, it sounds like Starbucks . And, hey, we’re not sure what the folks at the 1910-era Starbird Apartments around the block on Boylston will think.
One of the most recent Starbird openings was in Colorado (Image: Starbird Chicken)

The first Starbird opened in 2016 in Sunnyvale, California, on W El Camino Real a few miles from Apple Park and a shorter drive from the LinkedIn headquarters. The Silicon Valley debut served as the pilot location for the concept, testing their app-based curbside pickup model alongside standard dine-in service. Like most big chains, in-store ordering is heavily automated via digital kiosks and integrated mobile app check-ins.

Starbird’s traditional real estate footprint favors car-oriented, suburban-style corridors over dense, pedestrian neighborhoods but there a few different formats of stores. In San Francisco, Starbird developed a commercial ghost kitchen hub in SoMa, serving the area through bike and scooter couriers and delivery apps.
Capitol Hill, circa 2026 and 2027, is up to its ears in chicken joints. And the flock is growing even with the now permanent loss of neighborhood favorite Bok a Bok .

This month, CHS reported plans from Puget Sound-based Conscious Hospitality Group for a re-start of its 11th Ave restaurant space with a new roasted chicken venture fronted by celebrity influencer chef Matt Broussard . The Seattle Times gushed over the prospects but didn’t report that the plan is a re-heat. The 11th Ave space was originally the flagship location of the company’s scuttled “1,000 location,” sustainable, and tech-optimized chicken sandwich chain concept Mt. Joy.
Starbird, meanwhile, has pushed past the 20 location mark and is on a skyward trajectory.

“From day one, we saw something special in Starbird. This innovative concept is in a league all its own,” investor Greg Dollarhyde said in an announcement five years ago as the company raised $12 million in funding. “Starbird continues to beat every expectation.”
Starbird Capitol Hill is under construction at 600 E Pike. Learn more at starbirdchicken.com .

articles.title: Here are your chances to speak up on the mayor’s proposal to overcome Seattle’s $175M deficit
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: The Seattle City Council has launched its review of Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed $9.1 billion 2027–2028 budget, scheduling multiple hearings and public comment opportunities over the next two months before adopting a final plan.

Councilmember Dan Strauss , chair of the Select Budget Committee, emphasized community participation as the council evaluates funding priorities. Residents can weigh in during six regular comment sessions and two dedicated public hearings featuring both remote and in-person testimony.

CHS reported here on the Wilson proposal which would wipe out an inherited $175 million deficit without tax increases or withdrawals from city reserves. The proposal would cut roughly $50 million annually in General Fund spending by eliminating 128 positions and aligning departmental budgets with historical costs, pairing these cuts with $50 million in shuffled funding — primarily leveraging JumpStart payroll tax revenues to cover core services and homelessness programs — and enabling the city, Wilson says, to project balanced budgets through 2030 without drawing on reserves.
The council’s announcement invites the public to review the council’s Budget Basic webpage to “learn more about how they can make their voice heard.”

articles.title: Primetime Mines Comedy from the Sordid Series To Catch a Predator
articles.author: Kathy Fennessy
paras: Tall, blandly handsome Chris Hansen began as a TV reporter like any other. He cut his teeth on regional stories before hitting the big time when he joined NBC News as a correspondent before becoming a regular contributor to Dateline NBC . So far, so good, but run-of-the-mill reporters don’t find themselves the focus of high-profile feature films, like Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime .

No, Hansen was something else. When NBC tapped him as host of Dateline ’s spinoff series To Catch a Predator in 2004, he became iconic: a hero to viewers who saw nothing hinky about sting operations involving paid actors, a villain to viewers who found the whole thing sleazy as hell, and a gift to Saturday Night Live and The Simpsons , because the show was rife for parody.

The setup was remarkably simple, at least on the surface. Members of Perverted-Justice, To Catch a Predator ’s volunteer-run partner organization, would catfish male adults by posing as underage girls and boys on online message boards in order to arrange sexual encounters.

With NBC’s resources, suburban rentals across the country would be staged to look like family homes. The “decoy,” a male or female actor in their 20s, would greet the guest while hidden cameras captured their small talk, but the minute things took a sexual turn, Hansen would emerge from the shadows like an off-duty David Caruso, circa CSI: Miami , before reading quotes from the chat transcripts, followed by a verbal beatdown, then a tension-relieving “You’re free to go,” only for waiting police officers to arrest the man for online solicitation of a minor.

Though the decoys and locations would change, the ruse could only go on for so long, since word would get out whenever the 40-person crew came to town. Just as sexual predators could use message boards to meet minors, they could also use them to warn other predators.

But that isn’t what killed the series. To show what did, screenwriter Ajon Singh adapted the 2007 Esquire article “Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die,” but instead of focusing on the Texas man (played by actor/director Alex Winter, a child sexual abuse survivor) who would make the worst decision of his life, Oppenheim shifts between Hansen (a blond-tipped Robert Pattinson), producer Andie Bender ( Severance ’s Merritt Wever), and decoy Dan Plumb (Skyler Gisondo, Superman ’s Jimmy Olsen). Rather than a tragedy, it’s a horror satire in which Hansen, in his quest for ratings, becomes as harmful as the predators he aims to catch. In an entirely different way, of course.
NBC stuck with Hansen after the show came to a halt in 2007, but the network parted ways with him in 2013. Since then, YouTube has provided the home for his “news gathering,” as he calls it.

As for the actor who portrays him, Pattinson has continually challenged himself as an actor since his Twilight days, and it’s admirable, even if his reach can exceed his grasp. He has a tendency, for instance, to fade next to more powerful costars, like Guy Pearce in The Rover , Willem Dafoe in The Lighthouse , or Jennifer Lawrence in Die My Love . In Primetime , however, he rises to the occasion as a hollow man who believes his own hype. It’s the best work he’s done since David Cronenberg’s Cosmopolis , where he played another king-of-the-world type. He and Wever are particularly terrific together, possibly because she isn’t playing a romantic foil. As a performer, her earthy groundedness generates a compelling tension with his character’s studied slickness.

In a film filled with many shades of creep, including Matthew Maher as the founder of Perverted-Justice, Del (singer/songwriter Phoebe Bridgers) and Dan come closest to the good–or at least neutral–pawns in the game as aspiring actors just trying to get credits on their resumes and make a few bucks. With her white-blonde hair dyed dark brown, the barely-recognizable Bridgers makes a vivid impression in her most substantial role to date. I wish I could say the same of Anna Faris, but she’s wasted as Hansen’s neglected wife.

Considering his background as a documentarian, Oppenheim ( Some Kind of Heaven and co-director of the upcoming Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything ) has a sure hand with actors, and Primetime is plenty entertaining, if somewhat anticlimactic after David Osit’s 2025 documentary Predators , which covers similar ground, but without the glibness that often accompanies satire.

As a survivor of child sexual abuse himself, Osit takes a more nuanced approach to the subject, bolstered by unaired footage which shows some of these men in a different light, but instead of rehabilitation, Hansen presented public humiliation and criminal charges as their only options.

Osit’s ace in the hole was the sit-down interview with Hansen that concludes his documentary. Pattinson fully earns his flowers as an almost cartoonishly terrifying version of the guy, but there’s nothing quite like the real thing. As Hansen boasts, “What I do is for a greater purpose.”

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Quiet Zone in Kent
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On August 24, 2026, Kent’s long-awaited Quiet Zone took effect along the BNSF Railway mainline through downtown. This designation, granted by the Federal Railroad Administration in June , no longer requires trains to sound their horn when approaching an at-grade crossing. Over the past 14 years, the City of Kent has worked to meet the necessary requirements to achieve a Quiet Zone. Recent infrastructure upgrades include building raised concrete medians, adding additional signs, and refreshing pavement markings. In a non-Quiet Zone area, all trains are required to sound their horn 15-20 seconds before each street crossing.

The BNSF mainline tracks are used by 38 passenger trains and many more freight trains every day. The frequent at-grade crossings in downtown Kent resulted in nearby residents hearing hundreds of train horns day and night. The Quiet Zone stretches between S 212th St and S 259th St. The following crossings are included:

As safety is still a top priority, train engineers are still allowed to sound the horn in emergency situations or as they deem necessary. While the Quiet Zone is officially in effect, it may take some time for nearby residents to hear a difference. One week after the change was implemented, the Kent Reporter noted that many trains were still using their horn at each crossing. I was in Kent earlier this week and each of the five trains (four Sounder, one Amtrak Cascades) I saw used their horn at each crossing.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.
